title: Number of Submatrices That Sum to Target
description: Brute force to optimized: enumerating every rectangle via 2D prefix sums versus fixing row pairs, collapsing to 1D, and applying the Subarray Sum Equals K hashmap technique.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a rows by cols matrix and an integer target, return the number of non-empty submatrices (rectangles) whose sum is exactly equal to target.

blocks.text: Given matrix and target, count every rectangular block of cells whose sum equals target exactly, over every possible position and size.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Every Rectangular Region That Exactly Hits a Budget
blocks.text: Picture a grid of values, and needing to count every possible rectangular region whose total exactly matches a specific target number, not just gets close to it.

blocks.caption: Fixing row boundaries collapses the 2D search into a familiar 1D one

blocks.text: There are 4 submatrices summing to exactly 0, including single 0-valued cells and larger balanced regions.
There are 5 submatrices summing to exactly 0.

Before checking every rectangle's sum independently, notice that fixing a pair of row boundaries collapses the entire problem down to a 1D subarray-sum-counting problem, one already solved efficiently elsewhere.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For any fixed pair of top and bottom row boundaries, summing each column across just those rows produces a single 1D array, one value per column.

Observation 2: Counting rectangles within that fixed row range that sum to target is now exactly "count subarrays of this 1D array summing to target," the Subarray Sum Equals K problem.

Observation 3: That 1D problem is solved with a running prefix sum and a hashmap of how many times each prefix sum value has occurred, in linear time.

Observation 4: Repeating this for every pair of row boundaries, and summing the counts, covers every possible rectangle exactly once.
This leads to fixing every pair of row boundaries, collapsing to a 1D column-sum array, and applying the prefix-sum-plus-hashmap technique to count exact-target subarrays within it.
Build a 2D prefix sum grid so any rectangle's sum is a handful of lookups, then check every possible rectangle directly against target.

items: Build a 2D prefix sum grid, where prefix[i][j] holds the sum of the rectangle from the top-left corner to (i minus 1, j minus 1).
For every pair of a top-left corner and a bottom-right corner, compute that rectangle's sum using 4 lookups.
If the sum equals target, increment the count.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: every rectangle, checked directly against target

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The 2D prefix grid makes every rectangle sum a constant-time lookup, but all roughly (rows times cols) squared rectangles are still enumerated explicitly.
Each of the 4 corner boundaries is looped independently, covering every possible rectangle exactly once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows squared times cols squared), every rectangle is enumerated explicitly.
Space: O(rows times cols) for the 2D prefix grid.

Limitation: once a pair of row boundaries is fixed, the remaining search is really a 1D "count subarrays summing to target" problem, which has its own efficient O(n) solution, but the brute force still checks every column pair explicitly instead.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column pair per row pair is wasteful: for a fixed row range, the column search is exactly Subarray Sum Equals K on the collapsed 1D column-sum array, and that problem has a linear-time solution using prefix sums and a hashmap.

What replaces the inner double loop over columns: collapse each row range into one sum per column, producing a single 1D array, then count its subarrays summing to target using a running prefix sum and a hashmap of how many times each prefix sum has occurred.

The core idea: fix every pair of row boundaries, collapse to a 1D column-sum array, and apply the Subarray Sum Equals K technique to count exact-target subarrays in it, summing the counts across every row pair.

For each pair of top and bottom row boundaries, build a 1D array of column sums restricted to that row range. Walk that array with a running prefix sum and a hashmap counting how many times each prefix sum value has occurred; at each column, add the hashmap's entry for (current prefix minus target) to the total count.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: fix rows, collapse to 1D, count exact-target subarrays with a hashmap

blocks.text: Fixing a row range and collapsing it to one sum per column reduces the problem exactly to counting 1D subarrays summing to target, which the prefix-sum-plus-hashmap technique solves in one pass. Repeating this for every one of the (rows choose 2)-ish row boundary pairs, and summing the counts, covers every rectangle in the matrix exactly once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows squared times cols), one row-collapsing and hashmap pass per pair of row boundaries.
Space: O(cols) for the column-sum array and the hashmap.

blocks.text: This problem combines two techniques already used elsewhere on this sheet: fixing one pair of boundaries to collapse a 2D search into 1D, and the Subarray Sum Equals K prefix-sum-plus-hashmap technique to count exact-target subarrays efficiently in that reduced 1D array.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every rectangle", think: fix a row range, collapse to 1D, and reuse Subarray Sum Equals K.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(rows squared times cols squared) time and O(rows times cols) space. The optimized approach runs in O(rows squared times cols) time and O(cols) space.

items: Pattern: a 2D-to-1D reduction (fix row boundaries) combined with the Subarray Sum Equals K prefix-sum-plus-hashmap technique.
Core Idea: fix every pair of row boundaries, collapse each row range into one sum per column, then count 1D subarrays summing to target using a hashmap.
Time: O(rows squared times cols squared) for the brute force, O(rows squared times cols) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(rows times cols) for the brute force, O(cols) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: fixing row boundaries turns a 2D rectangle-counting search into a familiar 1D exact-sum counting problem.
Interview Difficulty: the 2D prefix sum brute force is straightforward; recognizing the Subarray Sum Equals K reduction is the higher-value insight.
One line memory trick: fix the rows, collapse to one column-sum array, then count with Subarray Sum Equals K.
